questions.question: In the opening verse 'Have you seen the one who denies the Din?', what does the word 'Din' primarily refer to according to the foundational tafsir?
options: Religion as a set of rituals only
The Day of Recompense and divine accountability
The collected teachings of the Prophet
questions.explanation: The foundational tafsir explains that 'Din' here primarily means the Day of Recompense and divine accountability. The verse asks whether the listener recognises the kind of person whose conduct shows no real belief in the coming Judgment.

questions.question: True or false: The Arabic verb 'yadu'u' in verse two describes mere passive neglect of the orphan rather than an active, forceful pushing away.
questions.explanation: The verb 'yadu'u' comes from a root meaning to push, shove, or repel with force. The tafsir stresses that this is not cold indifference but an active, violent rejection of a vulnerable child seeking help.

questions.question: Why is verse three's condemnation of one who 'does not urge the feeding of the poor' significant for ordinary Muslims?
options: It only applies to wealthy rulers and judges
It limits responsibility to giving from one's own wealth
It widens responsibility to include encouraging others to feed the needy
It excuses those who give in private
questions.explanation: The verb 'yahuddu' means to urge or motivate others. The tafsir notes that the verse condemns not only the one who refuses to feed the poor himself but the one who does not even use his voice or influence to encourage others to do so.

questions.question: True or false: Classical scholars including Ibn Kathir noted that the verse uses 'an salatihim' (away from their prayer) rather than 'fi salatihim' (within their prayer), and this distinction means the verse does not condemn the believer who merely struggles with wandering thoughts during salah.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir, citing Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibrahim al-Nakh'i among the Salaf, stressed that 'an salatihim' refers to wholesale neglect and disregard of the prayer, not to ordinary distraction within it. The believer who fights to maintain focus is not the sahun condemned here.

questions.question: Which of the following best reflects the classical Sunni scholarly debate over the meaning of 'al-ma'un' in verse seven?
options: Scholars unanimously held it referred only to gold and silver
Scholars debated whether it meant small household items lent to neighbours, zakat, or any beneficial assistance
Scholars universally limited it to formal Friday charity
Scholars treated it as a metaphor for prayer alone
questions.explanation: Imam Tabari and Imam al-Qurtubi record multiple opinions: small household utensils customarily borrowed by Arabs, zakat (held by Ibn Umar and Hasan al-Basri), and any beneficial item that is withheld. Qurtubi lists as many as seven distinct classical positions on this term.

questions.question: True or false: According to the contemporary tafsir drawing on Sayyid Qutb and Ibn Uthaymeen, riya (showing off in worship) is treated as a harmless personality trait rather than a serious spiritual disease.
questions.explanation: The contemporary tafsir cites the Prophet's description of riya as 'al-shirk al-asghar' (the lesser shirk). Sayyid Qutb describes it as the ultimate inversion of worship, and Ibn Uthaymeen taught that the test of sincerity is whether one would perform the act if no human could ever know about it.

questions.question: How does Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran characterise the warning 'Woe to those who pray' for modern audiences?
options: As proof that prayer itself is condemned in Islam
As a challenge to religious self-satisfaction, exposing prayer that is mere social convention without consciousness of Allah
As an instruction to abandon congregational prayer
As a verse limited to the hypocrites of Madinah with no contemporary application
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb describes the verse as one of the Quran's most searching challenges to religious self-satisfaction. He argues it is especially relevant where religion has become a social convention rather than a living encounter with the Divine grounded in accountability.
